blocks.text: If you're trying to picture the City2Surf course before race day, here's the route the way I'd talk you through it as a local — section by section, from the city start to the Bondi finish. For the official downloadable map with water stations and split points, head to city2surf.com.au; what follows is the lay of the land.
The course, section by section

items: Start — near Hyde Park, at Park and College Streets in the CBD, then a fast downhill along William Street.
Kings Cross — through the tunnel and out toward the harbour; this early stretch is quick, so don't get carried away.
Rose Bay — along New South Head Road beside the water. Enjoy it, because the hill is next.
Heartbreak Hill — an approximately 2 km climb from Rose Bay up to Vaucluse. This is the halfway point and the toughest part of the day.
Vaucluse to the coast — onto Old South Head Road and Military Road, with a few short sharp pinches before a rewarding downhill and big ocean views.
Bondi finish — a turnaround near Curlewis Street and roughly a final kilometre of flat switchback to the line on Queen Elizabeth Drive above the beach.

blocks.title: Reading the profile
blocks.text: The first few kilometres are net downhill and deceptively fast. The climbing is concentrated in the middle around Heartbreak Hill — and there are more little rises after it — so plan your effort to peak through the hills, not before them.
Best spots to watch or push hard

Rose Bay and the foot of Heartbreak Hill are my favourite places to spectate — the crowd support there genuinely carries runners up the climb. If you're racing, treat the top of the hill at Vaucluse as your cue to reassess your pace, and remember the sneaky final switchback at Bondi before you spend everything.

items.q: Where can I get the official City2Surf course map?
items.a: From the official site, city2surf.com.au, which publishes the current downloadable map with water stations, drink stations and split points.

items.q: Where does the City2Surf start and finish?
items.a: It starts near Hyde Park in the Sydney CBD (Park and College Streets) and finishes on Queen Elizabeth Drive above Bondi Beach, 14 km later.

items.q: How much of the course is uphill?
items.a: The signature climb is Heartbreak Hill, about 2 km from Rose Bay to Vaucluse near halfway, but there are also several shorter rises afterward before the downhill to Bondi.

blocks.text: People ask me this more than you'd think, usually with one eyebrow raised: are there snakes in Bondi? I always give the same answer — only one, and his name is Blake.

If you've wandered down Blair Street lately, you might have spotted a curious creature slithering along the footpath. Don't panic — this isn't the sort of snake that sends you running. He's the friendliest serpent in Sydney: Blake the Blair Street Snake, a community art project made entirely of painted rocks.

It starts with a single boulder — Blake's cheerful head, painted minty green with pink and black patches, perched beside a hand-lettered sign that reads: "I'm Blake the Blair St Snake. Add a painted rock to see how long I can get :)"

From there, a colourful line of rocks winds down the stone wall like scales on a giant, happy reptile. Some are splashed in pastels, others flecked with stars or faces, and a few were clearly painted by very small and very enthusiastic hands. Every week Blake stretches a little further as locals and passers-by add to him.
Why I love stumbling across Blake

In a world of "Do Not Touch" signs and endless screens, here's a simple invitation to join in. No permissions, no forms — just grab a rock, grab some paint, and make your mark. I've watched joggers pause mid-stride to admire him before carrying on toward the beach, and I've never once seen someone walk past without smiling.

Each rock tells a tiny story: maybe painted on a rainy afternoon, maybe made at a weekend craft session, maybe left by a visitor who wanted to be part of something local. To me, Blake is like Bondi's community diary — only instead of words, it's written in colour. Bondi's famous for its shimmering water and perfect surf, but this quirky reptile has become just as iconic in his own way.

If you're bringing kids, paint a rock at home the night before and let it dry — then it's ready to add to Blake's tail on the day. A weatherproof outdoor paint or a coat of clear sealer helps your rock survive Bondi's sun and salt air.

items.q: Are there actually dangerous snakes at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Bondi is a busy urban beach, so you're extremely unlikely to encounter a wild snake on the sand or promenade. The only "snake" locals talk about is Blake, the painted-rock art trail on Blair Street.

items.q: Where exactly is Blake the Blair Street Snake?
items.a: Along the stone wall on Blair Street in Bondi. Look for the minty-green painted boulder with the sign inviting you to add a rock — the trail of rocks grows from there.

items.q: Can I add my own rock?
items.a: Yes — that's the whole idea. Paint a rock, bring it down to Blair Street, and add it to the end of Blake's body to help him grow a little longer.

blocks.text: So next time you're wandering Blair Street, keep an eye out. Bring a rock, add your touch, and help Blake slither a little further. Because yes — there is a snake in Bondi. Just one. And he's the kind that makes everyone smile.

The City2Surf draws tens of thousands of runners every August for its atmosphere, its city-to-sea course, and one very famous hill. Whether it's your first or you're chasing a personal best, a bit of preparation goes a long way. Here are the ten things I'd tell any mate before they line up.
1. Know the course

It's 14 km from the CBD to Bondi. The opening kilometres are fast and net downhill, then around the middle you hit Heartbreak Hill — roughly a 2 km climb from Rose Bay to Vaucluse. Knowing where the hill sits helps you save energy for it instead of blowing up early.
2. Enter early and pick the right wave

Entries open earlier in the year and sell out — the 2026 event sold out well before race day. Register as soon as entries open, and choose a start wave that matches your realistic finish time so you're not weaving through slower runners (or holding up faster ones).
3. Train for the hill

Heartbreak Hill is what people remember. Add hill repeats to your training once a week in the lead-up so both your legs and your head know what a sustained climb feels like. It's the single best thing you can do for your time.
4. Build up gradually

Increase your weekly distance slowly rather than cramming. A mix of one longer run, some faster efforts and easy recovery jogs beats a couple of heroic long runs. Consistency is what gets you to 14 km comfortably.
5. Sort your hydration and fuelling

Hydrate in the days before, not just on the morning. Have a light, familiar breakfast a couple of hours before the start. Whatever gels or drinks you plan to use, practise with them in training first.
6. Gear you've tested — and sunscreen

Wear well-broken-in shoes and light, moisture-wicking clothing. Nothing brand new on race day. And even in August, put on sweat-resistant sunscreen before the start — the sun really shows up by the time you reach Bondi.
7. Plan your transport

Roads close and the nearest stations fill early. Give yourself a solid hour of buffer to get to the start, find the gear check, queue for the loo and warm up. Public transport beats driving every time on race day.
8. Check the weather

Early-August Sydney can swing from cool and grey to surprisingly warm. Check the Bureau of Meteorology forecast and dress accordingly — a cheap layer you can shed at the start line is a good friend on a cold morning.
9. Pace it in thirds

Start conservatively, run the hill on effort rather than staring at your pace, and use the downhills to recover without over-striding. Break the run into thirds and reassess how you feel at each. Negative-splitting the City2Surf feels a lot better than fading.
10. Recover and celebrate

Keep walking for a few minutes after the line rather than stopping dead, grab water and a snack, and agree a meeting spot with your crew in advance — phone signal gets patchy in the crowd. Then reward yourself: brunch, a swim, or a dip at the Icebergs pool. You've earned it.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf and how hilly is it?
items.a: 14 km, and hillier than first-timers expect. The main climb is Heartbreak Hill, about 2 km from Rose Bay to Vaucluse near halfway, with a few more short rises after it.

items.q: Do City2Surf entries sell out?
items.a: Yes — it's very popular and sells out ahead of race day, so enter early through city2surf.com.au and pick a start wave matching your expected finish time.

items.q: What should I not do on race day?
items.a: Don't wear or eat anything you haven't tested in training, don't go out too fast, and don't skip sunscreen — the Sydney sun is strong by the Bondi finish.

blocks.text: The blokes and women in the blue-and-yellow are the reason half the world knows Bondi at all. I get asked about them constantly — who's the boss, is so-and-so still here, are they actually real? So here's my local rundown of the Bondi Rescue lifeguards, who they are, and how the team really works.

First, the thing people are always surprised to learn: they're real. The lifeguards you see on Bondi Rescue are genuine professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council, patrolling Bondi year-round. The TV cameras just follow their actual working day. The show has been running since 2006, but these people were saving lives here long before the first episode aired — and they'll be here long after the cameras pack up.
The lifeguards you'll recognise from the show
The roster changes from season to season, but a handful of faces have become the heart of Bondi Rescue. These are the ones you're most likely to spot on the sand.
Bruce "Hoppo" Hopkins — head lifeguard

Hoppo runs the show — literally. He's the head lifeguard at Bondi, one of Australia's longest-serving, and he's been on the beach since the early 1990s. He was named Australian Lifeguard of the Year back in 2006, and he's appeared in every season of Bondi Rescue. Calm, no-drama, deeply respected by his team — if you only know one Bondi lifeguard, it's Hoppo.
Anthony "Harries" Carroll — senior lifeguard

Harries is the show's biggest personality and its most quotable rescuer, famous for throwing everything he has into a rescue. Off the beach he's spoken openly about overcoming dyslexia and bullying, and he's since written a children's book about that journey. Love him or find him a lot, he's Bondi Rescue's beating heart.
Trent "Maxi" Maxwell
Maxi is one of the most popular of the younger lifeguards and has become a familiar face well beyond the beach — he even co-authored a book of stories from the Bondi lifeguard team.
The wider crew

Plenty of other lifeguards have become fan favourites over the years — names like Deano, Whippet, Reidy, Kerrbox, Jesse and Chappo have all had their moments on screen. Some are veterans mentoring the next generation; others are up-and-comers earning their stripes in heavy surf. Between them they cover thousands of rescues a season.

blocks.title: They're working, not performing
blocks.text: When you see the lifeguards sprinting down the sand or launching a ski, give them room — that's a real emergency, not a scene. The best way to make their job easier is simple: always swim between the red-and-yellow flags.
So who's on the beach right now?

Because the team rotates and new lifeguards come through each season, the surest way to know exactly who's patrolling is to look for yourself — the lifeguards are on duty at the tower every day. For the current line-up featured on the show, the official Bondi Rescue broadcaster and Waverley Council's lifeguard service are the sources I'd trust over any fan list (including older versions of this page).

items.q: Who is the head lifeguard at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Bruce "Hoppo" Hopkins. He's the head lifeguard at Bondi, one of Australia's longest-serving lifeguards, and was named Australian Lifeguard of the Year in 2006.

items.q: Is Hoppo still on Bondi Rescue?
items.a: Hoppo has been the show's one constant — head lifeguard and a fixture in every season to date. He's the most recognisable member of the Bondi team.

items.q: Are the Bondi Rescue lifeguards real lifeguards?
items.a: Yes. They're genuine professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council who patrol Bondi year-round. The show films their real working shifts.

items.q: How many seasons of Bondi Rescue are there?
items.a: The series has run since 2006 and produced 18 seasons through 2024, making it one of Australia's longest-running factual TV shows.

blocks.text: Whether you're a fan of the show or just here for a swim, it's worth a quiet nod to the crew in the tower. They're the reason Bondi is one of the safest famous beaches in the world — and yes, they really are that good.

blocks.text: I hear it mangled at least once a day down at the beach, usually from a visitor asking directions. So let me settle it for you: Bondi is said "BON-dye" — the last bit rhymes with "eye", not "ee".

For Australians who grew up with Bondi, there's no question about it — but the spelling trips up overseas visitors, who very reasonably read the "i" on the end as "ee". It isn't. Think "bond" (like a secret agent) followed by "eye", with the emphasis on that first syllable: BON-dye.
What "Bondi" actually means

The name is Aboriginal. Waverley Council, which looks after the beach, records that Bondi comes from a local Aboriginal word meaning "the sound of the waves breaking on the beach" (you'll also see it given as "water breaking over rocks"). Once you know that, the name makes perfect sense — stand on the promenade for a minute and the meaning is all around you.
Easy way to lock it in: it rhymes with "Aussie hi" — Bon-dye, not Bon-dee. Get the ending right and you'll sound like you've been coming here for years.

items.q: How do you pronounce Bondi?
items.a: "BON-dye" — "bond" followed by "eye", with the stress on the first syllable. The "i" at the end sounds like "eye", not "ee".

items.q: Is it BON-dee or BON-dye?
items.a: BON-dye. "BON-dee" is the most common mispronunciation among overseas visitors, but locals say BON-dye.

items.q: What does Bondi mean?
items.a: It's from a local Aboriginal word. Waverley Council records the meaning as "the sound of the waves breaking on the beach" (also commonly translated as "water breaking over rocks").

blocks.text: Hope that helps — now say it with confidence and enjoy the beach.

Every August, my end of Sydney turns into a finish line. The City2Surf is the run that ends at Bondi, and whether I'm out on the course or cheering from the promenade, it's one of my favourite days of the year. Here's my local guide to running it well — and enjoying it.

The City2Surf is one of the world's largest fun runs — tens of thousands of people, from elite racers to first-timers in fancy dress, all making the 14 km journey from the city to the sea. It starts near Hyde Park in the CBD (at Park and College Streets) and finishes on the grass above Bondi Beach. Part race, part street party, it's Sydney at its most joyful.
The route — and yes, Heartbreak Hill

From the start you drop down William Street, through the Kings Cross tunnel, then out along New South Head Road with the harbour glinting beside you through Rose Bay. Then comes the bit everyone's heard about: Heartbreak Hill, a roughly 2 km climb from Rose Bay up to Vaucluse. It's the halfway point and the make-or-break section. From Vaucluse you head along Old South Head Road and Military Road before a glorious downhill toward the coast, a turnaround near Curlewis Street, and the finish on Queen Elizabeth Drive at Bondi.

blocks.title: Two things first-timers don't expect
blocks.text: Heartbreak Hill isn't the end of the climbing — there are several short, sharp pinches after it, so keep something in reserve. And don't empty the tank on the final downhill: after you reach the bottom there's still around a kilometre of flat, switchback running to the line. Save a little for it.
Getting there and home

Public transport is by far the easiest option — roads close across the eastern suburbs and parking near the start or finish is a nightmare. Bring an Opal card or tap on with a card or phone. For the start, trains to St James, Museum or Town Hall put you a short walk from the assembly area. Getting home from Bondi, there are usually free shuttle buses to Bondi Junction where you can pick up the T4 line back to the city. Because the exact shuttle and closure details change each year, I check Transport for NSW's event page in the days before.
My tips for a strong run

items: Train on hills. Even a few weeks of hill repeats makes Heartbreak Hill far less scary.
Go out easy. Aim to run the second half faster than the first — the crowd energy will tempt you to sprint the opening kilometres; don't.
On the hill, shorten your stride and hold a steady effort. People who charge past you early are usually the ones walking it near the top.
Don't experiment on race day — no new shoes, gear or energy gels you haven't tried in training.
At water stations, keep moving through rather than stopping dead; it keeps you and everyone behind you safe.
Sunscreen and a cap. It's August, but the Sydney sun still bites by the time you reach Bondi.

blocks.text: The finish (and the afterparty)

Crossing the line above Bondi Beach, salt air in your lungs and the ocean right there, never gets old. Once you've caught your breath, the celebrating begins — the Bondi pubs and the Pavilion turn on afterparties every year. I've written a separate guide to the best spots to recover and celebrate, and a companion piece on the things I wish I'd known before my first City2Surf.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf?
items.a: 14 kilometres, from Sydney's CBD (near Hyde Park) to the finish above Bondi Beach.

items.q: When is City2Surf 2026?
items.a: Sunday 9 August 2026. The 2026 event is sold out — for entries and future dates, check the official site at city2surf.com.au.

items.q: Where is Heartbreak Hill?
items.a: It's an approximately 2 km climb along New South Head Road from Rose Bay up to Vaucluse, at roughly the halfway mark of the course.

items.q: How do I get to the start and back from Bondi?
items.a: Use public transport — roads close and parking is very limited. Trains reach the CBD start; from the Bondi finish there are usually free shuttles to Bondi Junction for the train home. Check Transport for NSW for the current year's details.

blocks.text: Whether you're chasing a personal best or just want to say you've run from the city to the surf, City2Surf is a Sydney rite of passage. Train a little, pace it smart, and I'll see you at the Bondi end.

blocks.text: You've survived the 14 km from the city to the sea — now for the best part. The Bondi afterparty is a City2Surf tradition, and as a local I can tell you the whole beachfront turns into one big celebration the moment the runners start pouring in. Here's where I'd point you.

blocks.title: Get in early
blocks.text: Every good spot fills fast as tens of thousands of people flood into Bondi. By midday you're looking at long queues, so head straight from the finish to your chosen venue — or, if you're just here for the party, aim to be in place by around 11am. The specific line-ups, DJ sets and drink deals change every year, so check each venue's own socials for what they've got on this time.
The reliable Bondi afterparty spots
Hotel Ravesis

The long-standing go-to for runners and their support crew, right on the corner overlooking the beach. Those balcony tables are gold and go early — it's a short dash from the finish, so don't stop running just yet.
Royal Bondi
A Merivale venue that reliably throws one of the bigger, livelier parties, with DJs and a buzzing crowd. Always a safe bet for atmosphere.
Beach Road Hotel

"The Beachy" is a Bondi institution and often hosts the biggest afterparty of the lot. It's a little further from the finish, so it rewards those with legs left in them — and be warned, the queue can be the biggest too.
North Bondi Fish & North Bondi RSL

Up the quieter northern end of the beach, these two are my pick for views and a slightly more relaxed vibe. North Bondi Fish does the beachfront-dining thing with DJs and ocean views; the RSL next door is simply one of the best-value, most easygoing spots on Bondi for a post-race beer.
Hotel Bondi & the Bondi Pavilion

If your legs have completely seized up, Hotel Bondi sits close to the finish and is always lively. The Bondi Pavilion, right on the sand, also regularly hosts finish-line celebrations — worth a look for something a bit different.

items.q: Where's the best City2Surf afterparty in Bondi?
items.a: The perennial favourites are Hotel Ravesis and Royal Bondi near the finish, and the Beach Road Hotel a little further on for the biggest party. North Bondi RSL and North Bondi Fish are great for a more relaxed celebration with a view.

items.q: What time should I get there?
items.a: As early as you can — venues fill and queues build by midday. Head straight from the finish, or be in place by around 11am if you're just coming for the party.

items.q: How do I find out this year's events and deals?
items.a: Line-ups, DJs and drink specials change each year. Check each venue's own social media, or the official City2Surf channels, for the current year's finish-line events.

blocks.text: However you celebrate, pace the day like you paced the run — plenty of water between drinks, and soak up that unbeatable Bondi finish-line feeling. You earned it.
